sentences.text: First, the removal of the requirement that the Minister may issue an RO only after sending of notice and receiving of representation to the person within a 14-day period.

sections.label: Attorney-General's prosecution power
sections.summary: Under article 35(8) of the Constitution, the Attorney-General has discretionary power to institute, conduct or discontinue proceedings for any offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Under article 35(8) of the Constitution, it is the Attorney-General who has the power, exercisable at his discretion, to institute, conduct or discontinue any proceedings for any offence.

sections.label: MRHA orders not justiciable
sections.summary: Section 18 makes all orders and decisions under MRHA not justiciable, so courts cannot call them into question.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The final point, Sir, is on section 18: all orders and decisions made under MRHA are not justiciable, meaning it cannot be called into question by the Court.

sections.label: Court proceedings and religious hatred
sections.summary: Court proceedings are unsuitable for such matters as open proceedings may incite religious hatred, citing the Maria Hertogh riots.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Court proceedings would not be suitable to deal with such matters because they are open proceedings and may unwittingly incite hatred among different religious groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: And one good example of this is the Maria Hertogh riots which happened in the 1950s where a Christian judge ordered a girl, who was brought up in a Muslim community, be returned to her Christian biological parents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This caused riots in which 18 people died.

sections.label: Reasonable grounds and CLTPA detention
sections.summary: The focus is on process and reasonable grounds for the Executive's decision, as with CLTPA detention orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The focus is on the process and whether there are reasonable grounds to support the decision of the Executive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This is already the case for orders of detention made by the Minister under the Criminal Law Temporary Provisions Act (CLTPA).

sections.label: Offences, fines and imprisonment
sections.summary: It asks whether Parliament should create offences for breach of regulations prescribed by the Minister, instead of fines or imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: And I would welcome his views on this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: There is a reference to the creation of offences which shall be punishable with a fine not exceeding $5,000 or with imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or with both.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Would it not be better for Parliament to create the offences arising from breach of regulations that the Minister prescribes?

sections.label: Monitoring closed-door religious groups
sections.summary: It asks how groups meeting behind closed doors can be monitored for political causes, extremism, or unpermitted foreign speakers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: My concern is that, since we do not know what goes behind closed doors, the organisers may try to promote a political cause, or even impart extremist ideologies under the guise of religion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: How do we monitor such groups to ensure that they conduct their activities without breaking any laws, when regulators are unable to monitor what they say or communicate?

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Moreover, if foreign guest speakers are invited to speak without a permit, as would likely be the case given the private nature of the group, would this be against the law?

sections.label: Declaring foreign affiliations
sections.summary: It asks what happens if a local religious organisation is affiliated to an overseas organisation unapproved under local regulations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Once these amendments are made, local religious organisations are required to declare their associations or affiliations to foreigners or foreign organisations, if any.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: But what if the organisation is affiliated to an overseas organisation that is unapproved under local regulations?

sections.label: Rehabilitative initiative for racial remarks
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the initiative becomes mandatory for all offenders, including those who affected people with remarks on race and religion, and cites the Young Sikh Association's outreach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Had the incident simply ended with angry netizens heaping criticisms on her, there would only be tension and anger among all parties, and nothing constructive comes out of this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I hope this initiative can be made mandatory for all offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Certainly, those who may not have broken the law, but affected a group of people with their remarks in relation to race and religious matters, should be encouraged to take up the opportunity to learn from such initiatives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Religious organisations and communities can play their part in actively reaching out, like what the Young Sikh Association did.

sections.label: Mandatory declarations for foreign donations
sections.summary: The speaker asks MHA for evidence of past foreign influence through donations and how the $10,000 quantum compares with money laundering and terrorism financing monitoring figures.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, I would like to talk about the introduction of mandatory declarations for foreign donations of $10,000 per transaction to safeguard against foreign influence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Can MHA provide evidence or examples of past cases where foreign countries exerted influence and control over religious organisations through donations?

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: How is the proposed quantum compared with figures used, let us say, to monitor for money laundering activities or terrorism financing activities in Singapore?

sections.label: Leadership requirements for religious organisations
sections.summary: The passage states that governing bodies and top leaders of Singapore's religious organisations are required to be Singaporeans or Singapore PRs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Another concern is about leadership requirements placed on Singapore’s religious organisations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is stipulated that their governing bodies and top leaders are required to be Singaporeans or Singapore PRs.

sections.label: Exemption criteria transparency request
sections.summary: The speaker asks MHA to elaborate further on the criteria for exemptions so the process is more open and transparent.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Can I ask if MHA can elaborate further on the criteria for exemptions, so that this process is more open and transparent?

sections.label: Expanding IRO membership and collaboration
sections.summary: The speaker suggests IRO include other faith sect representatives and NSC coordinate interfaith groups, including developing religious educational materials for MOE.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Despite the occurrences of sensitive disputes, we are all Singaporeans, regardless of religion, and one has to acknowledge that all religions form part of our social fabric, too.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, perhaps the IRO can consider expanding its membership to include other faith sect representatives, so that we can work together towards a more inclusive society.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With the growth of interfaith organisations in Singapore, perhaps NSC can be the central body to bring these interfaith groups together to discuss how each organisation can work in synergy and be aligned with the national strategy and direction.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One of the potential areas of collaboration could be developing authentic religious educational materials for MOE to raise awareness in students.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Currently, there is no syllabus in schools imparting knowledge about our various religions.

sections.label: IRO inclusivity across faiths
sections.summary: The passage states that IRO should be as inclusive as possible with the various faiths to ensure religious harmony.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Next, IRO should be as inclusive as possible with the various faiths to ensure religious harmony.

sections.label: Minister's expanded powers, anonymous donations
sections.summary: Speaker supports the amendment allowing the Minister to make ROs against religious groups, but seeks assurances and flags concerns over anonymous donations.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: First, I support the need for immediate, pre-emptive and decisive actions to be taken to maintain racial and religious tolerance and harmony, and to remove threats to public peace and public order.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Hence, I support the amendment to allow the Minister to “make an RO against any religious group for the purposes specified in subsection (2A) if the Minister is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient” to do so.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: However, can the Minister give the assurance that: (a) the expanded powers conferred on the Minister are justified and grounded on relevant intelligence gathered and established facts; and (b) that no particular religious or racial groups would feel that they are being unfairly targeted?

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I understand the need for a “Know-Your-Donor” (KYD) process to be carried out, but the way in which “anonymous donation” is defined in the Bill may bring about potential disputes and loopholes.

sections.label: Competent authority qualities
sections.summary: The passage asks what qualities are expected of the competent authority that advises the Minister on RO matters.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: What are the qualities expected of this “competent authority” that provides advice to the Minister on matters pertaining to ROs?

sections.label: Support for the Bill
sections.summary: The speaker states that despite the clarifications sought, they support the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the clarifications I seek, I support this Bill.

sections.label: Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act
sections.summary: MRHA was enacted in 1990 to set principles for multi-religious co-existence, giving the Government powers against religious hatred and establishing the PCRH.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: MRHA was enacted in 1990 to lay out fundamental principles in a multi-religious society so that different religions can co-exist peacefully.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to the Act, the Government has the power to take actions against those who instigate hatred among religious groups, issue ROs and forbid them to make speeches to religious groups or distribute publications.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Act also established the PCRH which provides information and reports to the Government in relation to religious harmony matters.

sections.label: Rising radicalisation trend
sections.summary: According to MHA statistics, recent years have shown a rising trend of radicalisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to statistics from MHA, the past few years have seen a rising trend of radicalisation.

sections.label: Hours accumulated in 2018
sections.summary: In 2018, they accumulated more than 90,000 hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 2018, they accumulated more than 90,000 hours.

sections.label: Bursary awards and culture studies
sections.summary: SBF bursary awards benefit needy students of all backgrounds, and the speaker recommends culture studies lessons in schools.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: SBF awards annual Bursary Awards to needy students in primary and secondary school and junior colleges regardless of race or religion and this benefits students from all backgrounds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Also, initiatives, such as “Water For All” and guided mosque tours for non-Muslims, are testament to Masjid Al-Istighfar’s commitment to serving the community at large and strengthening interfaith relations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 2018, they accumulated more than 90,000 hours; the local community services clocked 31,740 hours and overseas services clocked 64,840 hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Other than MRHA, I do recommend that the Government implement “culture studies”.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Just like Social Studies lessons in schools, the culture studies lessons, integrated into students’ curriculum, could be a platform for discussions on the similarities and differences between each race and religion, thus fostering deeper connections and friendships among Singaporeans.

sections.label: Immediate removal orders and guidelines
sections.summary: The speaker supports immediate removal orders for offensive material and suggests clear guidelines and continued public outreach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Many recognise that it is, indeed, imperative for the Minister for Home Affairs to be given the authority to issue an RO to take effect immediately for the removal of offensive and subversive material.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The speed at which such material can be transmitted through today’s digital medium means that time is, indeed, of the essence and, where the seeds of such sensitive material are allowed to be sowed, it may be difficult, even impossible, to completely weed them out with the passage of time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Yet, there are always relentless cynics who would outcry this provision as one designed to curb freedom of speech and freedom of religion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It would, therefore, be beneficial if the Ministry can publish clear guidelines on what is likely to constitute subversive and offensive material, and it is also of paramount importance that discussion and outreach to the general public be continued unrelentingly.

sections.label: Safeguards against foreign interference
sections.summary: The proposed amendments provide safeguards against foreign actors interfering in Singapore's religious harmony.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: My final point on the amendments, and one which I personally think is especially crucial, is that the proposed amendments provides safeguards against foreign actors interfering in the religious harmony of Singapore.

sections.label: Singapore's religious diversity ranking
sections.summary: The Pew Research Centre this year identified Singapore as possibly the most religiously diverse country.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Singapore has been identified as possibly the most religiously diverse country on the planet by the Pew Research Centre this year.

sections.label: New citizens and workplace merit
sections.summary: New citizens must be educated on Singapore's values, and workplaces should progress people on merit rather than religious inclination.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: New citizens must, therefore, resonate the same chorus and must be educated on the values of Singapore – standing as one united people, regardless of race, language or religion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Having a workplace where people progress on merit rather than on religious inclination is a basic ingredient for employee happiness.

sections.label: Forward-looking legislation for Singapore
sections.summary: The speaker urges the Ministry to use such platforms and views the amended Act as forward-looking legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I, therefore, urge the Ministry to continue to utilise such platforms for the benefit of our people and for our nation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is my view that with the proposed amendments, the Act is now a forward-looking piece of legislation that will continue to provide a framework for Singapore to prosper as a nation.

sections.label: MRHA amendments and foreign influence
sections.summary: The MRHA amendments address new threats, requiring transparency on foreign donations and affiliations and majority Singaporean leadership.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: We are certainly not immune, notwithstanding that we have very good practices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I think the amendments made to MRHA are timely to deal with these new threats and the new challenges we face.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: One of the first measures that comes up very clearly is measures to control foreign influence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: By and large, they aim to promote transparency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: So, it has to be clear where these foreign donations come from, foreign affiliations have to be clearly disclosed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: At the same time, there is a requirement for the leadership, more than half of it to be Singaporeans.

sections.label: Offences and consequences in MRHA
sections.summary: Sections 17E and 17F cover serious offences such as urging religious violence or inciting religious hatred or ill-will.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Of course, for any legislation to have meaning, it must also clearly spell out offences and consequences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: And the more serious ones are in sections 17E and 17F for serious offences, including the urging of violence on religious grounds or inciting hatred or ill-will amongst religious groups.

sections.label: Community Remedial Initiative under section 16H
sections.summary: Section 16H lets the Minister offer a gentler penalty aimed at rehabilitation, resulting in a discharge not amounting to an acquittal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: One measure that I found quite interesting is CRI under section 16H which allows for the Minister to offer this option where certain offences have been committed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This is clearly a gentler penalty, and it looks to me like it is aimed at rehabilitation because the end result of this is the offender will get a discharge not amounting to an acquittal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I welcome the additional tool because it again allows for a more calibrated approach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: But I think it should also be clear that this does not mean we are going soft on people who incite ill-will or hatred.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I would also be grateful for the Minister’s clarification on whether this more calibrated toolkit with gentler options available also means that these tools may be used more often.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: If so, then it is important for the Ministry to have the resources necessary to monitor and take action.

sections.label: New and existing religious groups
sections.summary: The Bill's requirements will apply to all new as well as existing religious groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Alex Yam also asked whether the Act will forbid the entry of new religious movements if they do not have a local presence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But the requirements in the Bill, if it becomes legislation, will apply to all new as well as existing religious groups.

sections.label: MRHA scope and foreign interference
sections.summary: MRHA covers all religious harmony matters, with some Penal Code provisions moved over, while separate legislation addresses foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We took the view that MRHA should be comprehensive in covering all the matters relating to religious harmony, whether dealing with offensive speech or safeguarding against foreign influence that affects religious harmony, which is why we also moved some provisions from the Penal Code over.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We are looking separately into legislation to better counter foreign interference that is harmful to our national security and sovereignty.

sections.label: Assurance to religious groups
sections.summary: Religious groups are assured the requirements will be implemented practically and exemptions granted where needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They realised the need for the amendments in maintaining religious harmony.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have assured the religious groups that we will work with them, implement these requirements in a practical manner and, where needed, we will also grant exemptions.

sections.label: Ten thousand dollar donation amount
sections.summary: Ten thousand dollars was chosen because it was a significant amount by the standards of donations.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Ten thousand dollars was chosen because, by the standards of donations, it was a significant amount.

sections.label: Foreign and anonymous donations tracking
sections.summary: Mr Louis Ng asked whether foreign and anonymous donations are tracked; foreign donations to local religious organisations are not tracked now.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether we track foreign and anonymous donations.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We do not track foreign donations to local religious organisations now.

sections.label: Section 16G Competent Authority powers
sections.summary: Section 16G of the Bill gives the Competent Authority powers to ask for more information to determine accuracy of disclosures and check grounds for an RO.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Section 16G of the Bill gives the Competent Authority powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We can ask for more information to determine the accuracy of the disclosures and also to check whether there are grounds for an RO.

sections.label: Scope of the RO
sections.summary: The RO's scope only ensures every governing body member is a citizen or removes non-citizens; it cannot be used where a Singapore Citizen acts as a conduit for foreign influence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The scope of the RO only applies to ensure that every member of the governing body is a citizen, or to remove persons who are not citizens from the governing body.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Where a Singapore Citizen is acting as a conduit for foreign influence, we cannot use the RO.

sections.label: ROs reviewed by PCRH
sections.summary: The ROs will be reviewed by the PCRH, which makes recommendations to the President.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The ROs will be reviewed by the PCRH, which makes recommendations to the President.

sections.label: Purpose of 27-year-old law
sections.summary: The law has existed for 27 years and its success is shown by never having had to be used even once.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What is the purpose you seek to achieve?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have had this law for 27 years and the fact that it is successful is shown by the fact that we have not had to use it even once.

sections.label: Removing 14-day notice period
sections.summary: The new powers only remove the 14-day notice period, while safeguards and the exercise of powers stay the same.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Alex Yam asked how, in practice, these “new powers” can improve the effectiveness of curbing the spread of hate speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We are just removing the 14-day notice period.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But the safeguards and the exercise of the powers remain the same.

sections.label: Phrases not new
sections.summary: The phrases wounding of religious feelings and threat to public peace are not new.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: First, the phrases “wounding of religious feelings” and “threat to public peace” are not new.

sections.label: Amos Yee charged
sections.summary: Amos Yee made offensive remarks against Islam and Christianity repeatedly in 2015 and 2016 and was charged under section 298 of the Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Members will remember Amos Yee, who made offensive remarks against Islam and Christianity.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He did this repeatedly in 2015 and 2016, and so he was charged under section 298 of the Penal Code for uttering words with deliberate intent to wound religious or racial feelings.

sections.label: MRHA section 8 definition
sections.summary: Section 8 of MRHA sets out the definition and includes designated religious leaders: priests, monks, pastors, imams.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Section 8 of MRHA sets out the definition and includes designated religious leaders: priests, monks, pastors, imams.

sections.label: Private speech not covered
sections.summary: For people who are not religious leaders, private speech is not covered under the offences in section 17F.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For people who are not religious leaders, private speech is not covered under the offences in section 17F.

sections.label: Defence for religious leaders
sections.summary: The defence is tighter for religious leaders and requires showing the speech was private and the communication was domestic.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The defence is tighter for religious leaders and it requires two elements – first, that they show that it was private speech and, second, that the communication was domestic.

sections.label: ROs against addressing worshippers
sections.summary: ROs can be issued to stop a person from addressing a specified group of worshippers or members of a religious group.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: ROs can be issued to stop them from addressing a specified group of worshippers or members of religious a group.

sections.label: Action on religious breaches
sections.summary: Breaches known to the authorities will be acted on, especially egregious acts inciting religious violence or disharmony.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If there are breaches and if we know of these breaches, we will not hesitate to take action, particularly when we are alerted to an egregious act which incites religious violence or disharmony.

sections.label: RO, IMDA and POFMA
sections.summary: The RO in MRHA will not apply to online service providers that merely convey offending material; IMDA and POFMA powers can be used.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The RO in MRHA will not apply to online service providers that merely convey the offending material.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under the Broadcasting Act, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) can direct Internet Content Providers and Internet Service Providers to remove or block access to material that is prohibited under the Internet Code of Practice.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And if there is willful transmission of online falsehoods, then POFMA can be used.

sections.label: Non-participation in CRI
sections.summary: If a person chooses not to participate in the CRI, the person's conduct will be considered in deciding whether to prosecute.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the person chooses not to participate in the CRI, the person's conduct will be taken into account to determine if it is appropriate to bring criminal prosecution against him.

sections.label: CRI not used elsewhere
sections.summary: As far as is known, the CRI is not something other countries have implemented.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: No, the CRI is not something that other countries have implemented, as far as we know.

sections.label: Signal and 40,000 turnout
sections.summary: It sends a signal and message to all Singaporeans, and 40,000 people turned up there.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It sends a signal, sends a message to all Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There were 40,000 people who turned up there.

sections.label: Government neutrality among religions
sections.summary: Religious leaders must know the Government is neutral and fair to all religions, and religious harmony also depends on how Government leaders behave.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The religious leaders must know that we are neutral, and confidence has to be given to all religions that the Government will be fair and neutral and be the conscientious referee.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Members will see that religious harmony in Singapore is not only because of the laws but also because of how Government leaders have behaved.

sections.label: Civil and political rights
sections.summary: The law does not prevent them from exercising their civil and political rights.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The law does not preclude them from exercising their civil and political rights.

sections.label: Religious leaders supporting Bill
sections.summary: Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about religious leaders supporting the Bill and asked what views the Government would take if they had not been supportive.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about religious leaders supporting this Bill and she asked what views would the Government take if they had not been supportive of the Bill.

sections.label: Constitutional limits on religious freedom
sections.summary: Article 15(4) states freedom of religion does not authorise acts contrary to general laws on public order, public health or morality, and grounds for RO issuance are set out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Article 15(4) of the Constitution, which she may not have seen, states that the freedom of religion does not authorise any act contrary to any general law relating to public order, public health or morality.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, the Constitution itself recognises that there can be some constraints on the freedom of religion.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The grounds on which the RO can be issued to religious groups are in the circumstances that are set out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For example, foreign influence that undermines religious tolerance among different religious groups and that can present a threat to public peace and order in Singapore, and that is consistent with Article 15.

sections.label: Separation of religion and politics
sections.summary: The Member's third point is that he does not agree with the principle of separation of religion and politics, which was confirmed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The third point the Member makes, that he does not agree with the principle of separation of religion and politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I asked for confirmation that that is, indeed, what he said and my people say that it is, indeed, what he said.

sections.label: MP rejecting religion-politics separation
sections.summary: It is very surprising for an elected Member of Parliament to say he does not accept the principle of separation of religion from politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: How would Mr Faisal Manap feel if these were the views of the religion of the majority or the plurality, and that comes into politics?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, for an elected Member of Parliament in this House to say, "I do not accept the principle of separation of religion from politics", I think it is very, very surprising.

sections.label: National Steering Committee on Harmony
sections.summary: The National Steering Committee on Racial and Religious Harmony is chaired by Minister Grace Fu.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: One of them is the National Steering Committee (NSC) on Racial and Religious Harmony chaired by Minister Grace Fu.

sections.label: BRIDGE dialogue and education
sections.summary: BRIDGE seeks to provide safe spaces and opportunities for the public to engage in open, facilitated conversations on sensitive topics.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: One is Broadening Religious/Racial Interaction through Dialogue and General Education (BRIDGE) that seeks to provide safe spaces and opportunities for the public to engage in open and facilitated conversations on sensitive topics.

sections.label: Process for approving Restriction Orders
sections.summary: The Minister sends a proposed RO to the PCRH, which recommends to the President, so the Minister is not the sole approving authority.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Minister must send the proposed RO to the PCRH.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The PCRH then makes recommendations to the President, who can then decide whether to confirm, vary or cancel the RO.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, under the current process, the Minister is not the sole approving authority on the RO.

sections.label: Imam Nalla's 2017 supplication charge
sections.summary: In 2017 Imam Nalla made a supplication during a Friday prayer that was thought unacceptable; he was charged under the Penal Code and fined $4,000.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2017, in a slightly different context, Imam Nalla made a supplication during a Friday prayer in a mosque that we thought was unacceptable.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He was charged under the Penal Code, fined $4,000.

sections.label: Theseira on indiscriminate law use
sections.summary: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira said indiscriminate use of the law would create contention rather than consensus, and the law has not been used in 27 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira said that the indiscriminate use of the law would create contention rather than consensus.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And if Members look, the law has been there for 27 years, and it has not been used once.

sections.label: Policies and public support for harmony
sections.summary: Drawing lines, reinforcing positive norms and a series of policies, plus majority public support, have kept religious harmony in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We draw lines in the sand, reinforced positive norms and they made our society stronger.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is not just MRHA that has helped to keep religious harmony in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is a whole series of policies, approach and, most crucially, that a significant majority of our people accept, subscribe, support these policies and they want religious harmony.

sections.label: MRHA and natural state
sections.summary: The speaker says the current situation is not natural, noting nearly 30 years of the MRHA.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is not a natural state of things.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have had nearly 30 years of the MRHA.

sections.label: Muslim view on religion and politics
sections.summary: The speaker reads a paragraph on separating religion and politics and says he does not fully agree, as Islam encompasses politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: For that particular paragraph, I will read as full: "Tuan, satu lagi prinsip Akta ini adalah memisahkan agama dan politik.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: That means, I do not fully agree with the principle. "Sebagai seorang muslim", as a Muslim, "Islam difahami sebagai satu cara kehidupan atau A Way of Life" being taught, we learn that Islam is a way of life, of which Islam encompasses every aspect of life, including politics and the way to do politics.

sections.label: Accepting separation of religion and politics
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the person accepts the principle of separation between religion and politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Second, I think it might be easier to just cut to the chase and maybe tell me, do you accept the principle of separation between religion and politics or do you not accept it?

sections.label: Muslim cannot separate politics and religion
sections.summary: The speaker says that as a Muslim he cannot separate the two entities of politics and religion.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You said religion cannot be kept out of politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: That is what I meant that, me, as a Muslim, I cannot separate the two entities of politics and religion.

sections.label: Keeping religion apart from politics
sections.summary: The speaker agrees religion needs to be kept apart from politics so it is not used for personal or party benefit.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Would you agree that religion should be kept separate from politics in Singapore?

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: I do agree that religion needs to be kept aside, or apart from politics, so that religion will not be used to gain personal benefit or to benefit any political party.

sections.label: Five questions and CRI administration
sections.summary: The speaker reiterates five questions, saying none were captured in the Minister's reply, including how the CRI would be administered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
sentences.text: I raised five questions and I would just like to reiterate them because I do not think any of them was captured in the Minister's reply.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think the Member asked how the CRI would be administered practically and, more specifically, the sort of activities the Ministry has in mind.

sections.label: Due diligence defence
sections.summary: The Bill provides a due diligence defence for people who took reasonable steps to meet requirements.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill provides for a defence of due diligence where people can ensure that they took reasonable steps, exercised due diligence to ensure that they met the requirements.

sections.label: MRHA applies to religious groups
sections.summary: MRHA requirements apply to all these religious groups whether incorporated, registered, or not.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The MRHA requirements would apply to all these religious groups, regardless of whether they are incorporated, registered, or not.

sections.label: Law and rule of law
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the Government considers this at every stage and says the relationship should be structured on law and rule of law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And I hope as we move forward and the effectiveness of this Bill is assessed, that the Government consider that repeatedly at every stage because that is important.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I can assure Mr Pritam Singh that that remains my underlying belief – that relationship should be structured on the law and the rule of law, and exceptions should be carefully considered.

sections.label: Charging under section 17E
sections.summary: The man was charged, and charging under section 17E requires mens rea of knowledge and intention, so facts must be examined.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I am sorry that I left out answering that question.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But if I may say this, the man was charged.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Member is asking whether he can now be charged here under section 17E.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There are a number of requirements – mens rea of knowledge and intention and so, one has to go and look at the facts.

sections.label: Engaging religious bodies on secular space
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether religious bodies should be engaged to educate them that Singapore's secular space must be guarded, with religious values held as personal views.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
sentences.text: And in regards to that, would it be worthwhile, perhaps, engaging the religious body to drive across this point and to educate them that our secular space as a country has to be safely guarded and has to be guarded fundamentally, and that any religious values that we espouse in terms of religion as a way of lifestyle and so on, that can be held as a personal view.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We have extensive discussions with the religious leaders, both my Ministry but also the Government leaders, including the Prime Minister with the Christian leaders, the Catholic leaders, the Muslim leaders, the Mufti, Hindu Endowments Board.
